concepts.def: Grouping organisms by similarities to organise life and reflect evolution.
Linnaean groups: animals, plants, fungi, protists, prokaryotes.
Modern division (Woese): bacteria, archaea, eukaryota — based on RNA differences.
Two-part Latin name: Genus species (e.g. Homo sapiens).
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species (broad → specific).
Group of similar organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Characteristics & Classification — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Characteristics & Classification brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Characteristics & Classification.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The two-part Latin name of an organism is its:
options: family name
binomial name
domain
common name
Species
Genus
Kingdom
Class

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a silent and a missense mutation?
options: A silent mutation changes a base but the codon still codes for the same amino acid; a missense mutation changes the amino acid encoded.
Codons and anticodons are the same thing seen from two angles.
Missense and silent mutations always produce a non-functional protein.
A silent mutation has no effect because no base actually changes.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a codon and an anticodon?
options: Sucrose is pushed into the phloem by turgor pressure from leaf cells.
Codons and anticodons are the same thing seen from two angles.
A codon is a triplet of bases on mRNA; an anticodon is the complementary triplet on tRNA that pairs with it.
Codons are on DNA and anticodons are on mRNA.

mcqs.q: How is sucrose loaded into the phloem at a source?
options: By active transport (using ATP) via companion cells, against a concentration gradient.
Sucrose diffuses passively into the phloem because it is more concentrated outside.
Sucrose is pushed into the phloem by turgor pressure from leaf cells.
Missense and silent mutations always produce a non-functional protein.

options: They belong to the same species.
They belong to the same kingdom but different species.
They are in different genera.
